primary_claim: A trained toy model solving the Universal-AND problem learns a dense 'Binary Weighted Circuit' rather than the sparse construction proposed in prior theoretical work, providing empirical evidence that computational superposition occurs and offering a new explanation for why XOR is commonly readable from linear representations.
contradicts_or_qualifies: the sparse construction for the U-AND problem given in 'Toward A Mathematical Framework for Computation in Superposition' (CiS) — the author finds trained models instead learn a dense circuit
stated_future_work: explore inputs in superposition or input noise
explore loss using only a subset of AND pairings or uneven weighting for input co-occurrence
check whether RMS is a realistic way to score this
run the model over a sufficient range of parameters to establish scaling laws
look for similar circuitry in a real LLM
limitations_stated: toy models by their nature are not very representative of real situations
quote: It successfully learnt a solution to the problem, providing evidence that such computational superposition can occur in the wild.
